planting.note: Train young plants onto a wall, pergola, or fence in part shade in spring, in fertile soil with reliable drainage; grow two plants together for markedly better fruiting.

directions: Train young plants onto a wall, pergola, or fence in part shade in spring, in fertile soil with reliable drainage, since this evergreen twiner from central China resents waterlogging even though it tolerates low light well. Small, fragrant purple-and-white flowers open in spring and are followed in a good year by sausage-shaped purple fruits with sweet, translucent pulp, though fruiting improves markedly when two plants are grown together. Its leathery, trifoliate evergreen leaves make it a valuable year-round screen for shaded boundaries where deciduous vines would leave a winter gap. Prune after flowering to control its vigorous twining growth.

planting.note: Establish this Chilean rainforest vine in part shade against a sheltered wall or trellis in spring, in fertile, humus-rich soil; both a male and female plant are needed to set fruit.

directions: Establish this Chilean rainforest vine in part shade against a sheltered wall or trellis in spring, in fertile, humus-rich soil, since it is less cold-hardy than its Asian Lardizabalaceae relatives and appreciates protection from harsh winter wind. Deep maroon-purple flowers appear in winter, and because plants are typically dioecious, both a male and female specimen are needed to set the dark purple, sausage-shaped fruits filled with sweet white pulp. Its thick, glossy, evergreen trifoliate leaves make an unusual dense screen for shaded courtyards in mild coastal climates. Water regularly during establishment, then allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings once mature.

planting.note: Plant this Mediterranean evergreen clematis in autumn with its roots shaded and cool; prune lightly right after flowering.

directions: Plant this Mediterranean evergreen clematis in autumn with its roots shaded and cool while its ferny, sometimes bronze-tinted foliage climbs into brighter light above, the classic cool-roots-sunny-head rule relaxed here since the vine tolerates partial shade throughout. Nodding, bell-shaped cream to pale yellow flowers, often freckled maroon inside, open through winter into early spring when little else in the garden is blooming. It is a useful choice for softening a shaded wall or fence with off-season interest and a light almond scent in some selections. Prune lightly right after flowering to tidy growth without sacrificing next winter's buds.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring with roots shaded by mulch or low neighboring plants; prune only lightly and just after flowering.

directions: Set out container-grown plants in spring with roots shaded by mulch or low neighboring plants while the twining petioles climb a trellis or shrub toward filtered light. Creamy white to pale green flowers with a striking dark maroon-purple stamen cluster appear on the previous year's wood in late spring and summer, so prune only lightly and just after flowering to avoid cutting off next year's display. It is a more compact, semi-woody grower than many large-flowered hybrids, making it well suited to a shaded container or small trellis near a patio. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, especially through its first growing season.

planting.note: Plant against a sturdy wall, fence, or pergola in spring, tying in new growth as it develops since it climbs by leaning rather than by tendrils or twining.

directions: All parts other than the flowers should be treated as inedible, since this is a relative of the potato — grow it strictly as an ornamental screen. Plant this fast-growing, semi-woody scrambler against a sturdy wall, fence, or pergola in spring, tying in new growth as it develops since it climbs by leaning rather than by tendrils or twining. Large, fragrant clusters of blue-purple, star-shaped flowers with bright yellow centers open from summer into autumn and continue even in a partly shaded position, though bloom is somewhat fuller with a few hours of direct sun. Cut back hard in early spring where winters are borderline, since it often regrows vigorously from the base after cold damage.
